fixes.explanation: That's what the text says: Job cursed the day he was born (Job 3:1). His wife had told him to curse God and die (Job 2:9), but his words land on a day on the calendar instead. I think there's a lot of pain packed into that choice, friend. Hold on to that, because it matters as we keep going.

That's what his wife told him to do, not what Job does. She told him to curse God and die (Job 2:9). When Job finally speaks in Job 3:1, the text says he cursed the day of his birth. Her words and his words are two different things, friend.

The friends are right there, sitting with him for seven days and seven nights without a word (Job 2:13). But when Job breaks that silence, the text says he cursed the day of his birth. The day he was born is the target, friend, not anyone in the room.
Job asks for the opposite. He says, “May God above disregard it…” (Job 3:4). Disregard and remember point in opposite directions. I think Job is grieving his own birth here, friend.

Job asks that the night “…not appear among the days of the year…” and that it never be entered in any of the months (Job 3:6). I think that's what's underneath all this: Job wishes his life had never started. It's a heavy thing to hear, friend.

Job asks for the opposite. He says, “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.” (Job 3:7). He wants no joyful voice in that night. Go back and look at that verse again, friend.
That's what the text says. Job asks, “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.” (Job 3:7). He's asking for no joyful voice in it, not a crowd of them.

Job says, “For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest” (Job 3:13). Peace and rest are what he's longing for. After all he's been through, I bet rest sounds like the most beautiful word on earth.

Job says the opposite. He says of the captives, “they do not hear the voice of the oppressor.” (Job 3:18). In the place he describes, they don't hear that voice. I think that's part of the rest Job is longing for.

Job says, “The captives enjoy their ease; they do not hear the voice of the oppressor.” (Job 3:18). The captives are at ease, and the oppressor's voice doesn't reach them. So False is right, friend, because Job says they do not hear it.

Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). Small and great are both there, and the slave is freed from his master. Freed is the word Job uses, friend, and it fits the blank.

Punishment isn't in this verse at all. Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). The slave is released from his master. The word is freed, not punished.
Job says, “I sigh when food is put before me…” (Job 3:24). A plate of food is usually good news, and Job sighs at it. I think that tells you how heavy his days have gotten.
